Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01049

Someone may object: how could one nature turn into another unless something remained common to both—shared matter beneath the physical thing and its mental image? The philosophers compare this with prime matter, which has no definite character of its own but can become water, air, or fire when it takes on a form. They assume that there must be some shared matter behind all things. The answer is that a shared matter is needed when one feature or form changes into another, as black becomes white or an embryo develops into an animal. It is not needed when one whole nature changes into a different nature. The mind may suppose an undefined common element simply to picture the change. That is the main point of this scholar’s view.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01050

His contemporary, the well-known Mulla Dawwani, objected as follows. Anyone with ordinary good sense knows that one nature cannot turn into a different nature. What can change is matter taking on another form, or a subject taking on another quality. And anything that exists in the mind has no subject or container other than the mind, by virtue of existing in it. So the mind cannot change from being a mental quality into an external substance. What, then, is this one thing that supposedly has one nature outside the mind and another inside it? If its nature changes, in what sense is it still the same thing?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01051

It is also unclear what it means to say that existence comes before a nature. Even if that were granted, it would not allow one nature to become another. An added feature, whether it comes before or after another feature, does not change the nature it belongs to. If the nature changed, what exists in the mind would differ in kind from what exists outside it, contrary to the proof for mental existence. To say that a nature can exist in the mind either unchanged or transformed is like saying that Zayd can be in a house and either remain Zayd or turn into Amr.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01052

It is clear that if one thing turns into another, something must remain common to both, such as matter or a general kind. If nothing remains, it is false to say that one thing has become another. Simple good sense is enough to show this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01053

A supporter of the copy-and-shadow view could also say that an external thing can exist in the mind only through its image or shadow. The image could become the external thing if it were to exist outside the mind; in fact, this supporter already says that the image is not the thing itself. The same problem arises for this scholar’s view. If a mental quality keeps its mental nature when it exists outside the mind, it remains a mental quality and not a substance. If a mental idea of a substance exists in the mind, it remains a substance in the mind. Nor is the mental quality hidden from external reality: as a state of the soul, it already exists in the world, like other qualities of the soul. If it remains a mental quality outside the soul, it cannot become a substance merely by being elsewhere. Indeed, a mental quality existing apart from a soul is impossible, while a substance is possible. If the scholar means that the quality becomes a substance only by changing its nature, then the copy-and-shadow view can make exactly the same claim.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01054

The strongest version of the scholar’s reply is this: each external nature has a special relation to its mental image, and the mind recognizes that relation. The image is called the mental image of that nature because, if it existed outside the mind and changed into its external nature, it would be that very nature. But this does not mean that the existence of one thing is the existence of another. There is a difference between saying “If A existed outside the mind and changed into B, it would be B” and saying “If A existed outside the mind, it would be B.” In the first statement, the change from A to B is part of the claim; it is missing from the second.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01055

Someone may object that a mental quality would remain a mental quality even if it existed outside the mind. The reply is that this misses the claim. The claim is only that it would exist outside the mind. That kind of existence itself would change its nature, because a mental nature depends on existing in the mind, while an external nature depends on existing outside it. In short, a mental thing’s existence outside the mind means that its nature changes into an external nature, or at least includes that change. This needs careful thought; there are problems with it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01056

There is another explanation of the scholar’s view. It is closer to the truth and avoids some of these problems. External things have essential features that bring about their proper effects. For example, a body has dimensions and occupies space; a plant form enables growth and nourishment. When these natures exist in the mind, they become qualities of the mind, while their essential features remain in some way. Their images are now mental qualities.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01057

On this account, general natures are like prime matter as the first teacher and his followers describe it: in themselves they are not yet definite or fully formed, and so do not belong to any one basic kind. They become distinct natures only when considered in relation to one of the two modes of existence. Water, for example, is a flowing, wet, heavy body when it exists outside the mind. When it exists in the mind, it becomes a mental quality. In itself, apart from either mode of existence, it is not fully defined as either a body or a mental quality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01058

Someone may object that this does not agree with the accepted principles, because a thing cannot lose its essential features in either mode of existence. Nor can one thing have two modes of existence. The reply is that if existence comes before nature, then apart from its mental or external existence a thing has no definite nature at all—not substance, quality, or even an undefined nature. Once it exists, its mode determines what it is. If it exists without depending on a subject, it is a substance; if it depends on a subject, it is a quality. In the same way, if it can have dimensions, it is a body; if it can grow and be nourished, it is a plant, and so on. We can draw out these essential features only by considering the thing as existing outside the mind, either actually or by supposition. If we consider it only as existing in the mind, we can draw out its mental qualities, such as knowledge and other features of the mind. If we consider it without choosing either mode of existence, we cannot point to it or assign it a definite nature.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01059

The claim that essential features remain through the change from one mode of existence to another has another meaning here. The mind considers the mental image not as a quality that exists in the mind, but as a way of looking at the external nature. It can then judge the image by the features of that nature. For example, the idea of water in the mind is not itself a body, fluid, wet, or heavy. It is a mental quality. Yet the mind can consider it as water existing outside the mind and judge it by the features of external water.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01060

When the mind sets aside what distinguishes one body of water from another, it gains a power of insight beyond the senses. It sees a single reality from which particular waters arise and grasps an idea that applies to them all. The mind uses this idea as a mirror to learn about their external features and draws out their essential features as we have explained earlier. That is what we wanted to say in making sense of this scholar’s view.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01061

Know that most later thinkers do not build their views on sound spiritual principles or on firm, inspired insights. They rely instead on what might be logically possible and on ideas accepted without proof, not on deep experience or clear demonstrations. So when they try to give a deeper explanation, they add objections and replies until their books become layers of darkness. Only a few find a way out. God has not wronged them; they have wronged themselves.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01062
V. A solution drawn from higher knowledge
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01063

Here is another way to answer some objections to the claim that things can exist in the mind. It avoids having to say that a thing’s nature turns into a different nature. It also avoids the view of a respected contemporary scholar, who says that calling knowledge and mental forms “qualities” is only a figure of speech or comparison. At the same time, this account preserves the principle that a thing’s essential features remain the same even when its mode of existence changes, and it treats mental forms as real qualities. Here is the idea: the human soul can draw general ideas from things outside the mind, from what we imagine, and from images that are not physical things.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01064

When the soul draws one of these ideas, it is affected by a mental quality: its knowledge of the thing. A new quality therefore arises in the soul when it understands that meaning. The philosophers say that when we look within as we think, we find only this image. So the mental quality is the image itself, present in the soul and describing it. That is why they define knowledge as an image of a thing formed in the mind. But proof shows that real things are present in the mind, not in the way they exist outside it. This made it seem that knowledge of anything in a given basic kind must itself belong to that kind. The matter became difficult, and the truth unclear. Here is the right way to understand it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01065

Just as a particular person, such as Zayd, exists outside the mind along with his features—being white, laughing, walking, sitting, growing, an animal, and rational—so these features are real through Zayd’s existence. The Zayd we meet outside is the very person who laughs and writes, and who is an animal and rational. Zayd is a substance by his essential nature. But “substance” is not thereby essential to each way we describe him—as a writer, as someone who laughs, or as a rational being.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01066

The same is true of what exists in the mind. Universal knowledge is one of the realities found there. An instance of knowledge becomes definite when it joins with the reality of the thing known. Compare this with a body. Outside the mind, a body has size, shape and position. It may grow or remain without growth; it may be an element or a heavenly body. These features make it a particular kind of body. In the same way, knowledge becomes definite and actual by joining with the reality of what is known. Knowledge is its closest kind, while quality is a more distant kind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01067

Knowledge becomes actual and definite only when the reality of the thing known joins with it, so that in fact they form one reality that matches the thing known. This one reality is knowledge by its closest kind, quality by a more distant kind, and belongs to the basic kind of the thing known because of what makes it definite. Just as Zayd outside the mind is an animal by his closest kind and a substance by a more distant kind, while his particular features place him under kinds such as relation, quantity, and quality. The thing known and knowledge are united as a feature is united with the thing it describes. So knowledge belongs to quality, and quality is essential to it as knowledge; in reality, however, it is the very reality of the thing known. This answers the objection: knowledge is a state of the soul, so it must belong to quality; but if the nature of the thing known exists in the mind, it must belong to the kind of that thing too. That would seem to place one reality in two kinds.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-01068

The point is that knowledge belongs to quality in its own right, because quality is its closest kind. In the mind, the idea of the thing known is one with knowledge in reality and existence, so it belongs to the kind of the known thing only indirectly. Just as Zayd is a substance in his own right, but belongs to the kind called relation when we consider him as someone’s father or son. That accomplished scholar, following the earlier philosophers, holds that a quality and the description based on it refer to the same reality, though we can think of them in different ways. For him, “white” and “whiteness” are one reality, though we can consider one as describing a thing and the other as whiteness in itself. As you will see later, this point is explained more fully. It clears the difficulty and removes the confusion.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01069
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01070
I. What linking existence means
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01071

Someone may object: if existence is a link in a statement such as “A is B,” then B must exist in itself too. For something to exist for another thing, the objection says, it must first exist in itself. And if B’s being true of A is itself true of A, then that new link must also be true of A, and so on without end.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01072

We can clear up this difficulty by recalling a distinction made earlier. When the word “existence” means the link in a statement, it does not mean existence in general or existence as a feature established for another thing. These two uses are easily confused. Sometimes 'existence' means no more than the link between a subject and what is said about it, like the word 'is' in a sentence. We do not treat that link as a separate thing. This is called linking existence. At other times it means that something is real, either in itself or through another thing. We can call this second sense dependent existence, to distinguish it from the link itself.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01073

So “A is B” does not mean that B first exists on its own and then exists for A, as a color or form exists in the thing it belongs to. It means only that A has the feature B; “is” links the two. The subject can therefore be described by something that does not exist outside the mind, such as a lack or absence, while still having some standing in thought. As we have already seen, an endless series formed by our successive acts of attention and imagination is not impossible: it stops when we stop paying attention.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01074

Unless we consider both sides of a judgment, no link forms between them for us to judge that one belongs to the other. When we say “A is B,” we understand that B belongs to A as a way of seeing what A and B are like; we do not focus on the link itself. So in making this judgment, we cannot also ask whether B’s belonging to A belongs to A, or whether it is itself linked to A. In the statement “A is B,” the link is just a link. A link, simply as a link, cannot itself be linked to something else.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01075

But suppose we now say, 'The link between A and B has this feature.' We have stopped using that first link merely to connect the two terms and have begun thinking about it as a thing in its own right. It no longer serves only to connect the two sides; we can now treat it as one side of a new judgment and consider another link. That second link lets us consider the first, though we do not focus on the second link itself. If we then focus on it and say, “the link to the link is such-and-such,” we turn away from the original two sides and connect the second link to a subject. This creates a third link that we are not directly considering. If we then turn our attention to that link, we get a fourth, then a fifth and a sixth, and so on. The series ends when we stop making these voluntary shifts of attention.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01076

The great philosophers of earlier times said that a predicate, simply as a predicate, has no existence of its own apart from its being true of its subject. They did not mean that its existence in itself is exactly the same as its existence in its subject, as with qualities and forms. A predicate, simply as a predicate, is not a thing that first exists in itself and then belongs to a subject. They meant that it does not exist on its own; it is only true of its subject, and that is all its existence consists in.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01077

There is a difference between saying, “A quality’s existence in itself is the same as its existence in its subject,” and saying, “Its existence in itself consists in its being true of its subject.” The first claims that the quality has an existence in itself; the second does not. This argument concerns only what a compound statement means. Whether the two sides of the judgment must, in reality, exist in some way is a separate question.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01078

In our philosophy, every possible being exists only through its link to God's existence. I shall explain and prove this point later. It goes further than what some leading religious thinkers and great philosophers have said. They said that material natures exist in themselves in the very way they exist for their matter; that an effect, simply as an effect, exists for its cause; and that every lower being exists in the presence of the higher being that encompasses all the lower levels. On their view, all possible beings—both material things and beings free of matter—exist not for themselves but through something above them all: God, the One who must exist.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01079

Those great thinkers could not go beyond this kind of oneness: for them, a possible being has dependent existence, but it is not itself a link. They speak of existence besides God's, and so treat possible beings as having their own distinct existence. It is connected to God and attributed to Him, and it can never be separated from that connection. But through God’s grace we have proved—and will explain later—that a possible being’s existence cannot be split into an existence plus a separate link to the Creator. The being is itself a link to God: it is connected to Him in its very being, not by an added relation. In their view, a possible being has an existence that depends on God. In ours, the being is itself a link to God. We have already pointed out the difference between these meanings and the different terms for them, so they will not be confused just because the same word is used for both.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01080

One respected scholar of a later generation tried to reach the heights attained by the mystics and the great philosophers. In a treatise called al-Zawrāʾ, devoted to the unity of existence, he wrote: blackness, considered as a state of a body, exists; considered as an independent thing, it does not. A garment exists as a form in cotton, but if considered a thing separate from cotton, it cannot exist in that respect.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01081

Use this as a guide to all realities, he says, and you will understand the claim that the fixed essences have never even caught the scent of existence: they have never appeared and never will; only traces of them appear. Those are his words. He added other chapters, but none is stronger or clearer than this passage.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01082

How can he claim to fly to the sky on such weak wings? The confusion in this account is plain to anyone who has studied these subjects closely. Has he not confused dependent existence with linking existence? When we say “the body is black,” the word “black,” as the predicate in this statement, exists only as something said of the body. But that does not prevent blackness from existing in another way, when we are not considering it simply as a predicate in a statement—even if its existence in itself is the very same existence it has for the body.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01083

He says that blackness does not exist as an independent thing. If he means that blackness is not a substance, he is right: a quality cannot be a substance. But this is not the only way to consider blackness. We can consider it as a quality in itself, apart from its role as a feature of something. There is no doubt that its relation to a subject is not part of what blackness is when we consider it simply in itself.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01084

If he means that blackness, considered according to its own nature, does not exist, then we cannot accept that. A quality has existence in itself, just as a substance does. The difference is that a quality’s existence in itself is the very same as its existence for the thing it belongs to. A substance exists in itself and for itself. A quality exists in itself, but not for itself; it exists for another thing. As we said earlier, to exist for itself means not to depend on another thing.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01085
II. When existence is called a second-order concept, and what that means
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01086

Philosophers use the term 'second-order concept' in two ways. In the first sense, it refers to descriptions we form by thinking about things and the ideas from which we draw those descriptions. These include abstract nouns, features that necessarily follow from a thing’s nature, and relations between things. At other times, it means concepts studied by logic, such as “universal,” “particular,” and “kind.” These apply to concepts already in the mind, and statements made with them are themselves mental statements. These are the subject matter of logic, unlike the first group. In the first sense, the abstract idea of “existence” or “being real”—not existence itself as a reality—is a second-order concept. So are “thinghood,” possibility, necessity, and the terms derived from them. They are second-order concepts in metaphysics, not in the logical sense.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01087

More strictly, second-order concepts in logic are those that apply to first-order concepts as they exist in the mind. Their being in the mind is part of the setting for the judgment, not part of what is being described. This is what philosophers mean when they say that second-order concepts depend on first-order ones. Existence, thinghood, and similar concepts do not belong to this group.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01088

Questions about whether such concepts exist in the mind or outside it, and whether they help us reach new knowledge, belong to general philosophy. It has shown that a general concept can be a species, a broader kind, a difference, a special feature, or a common feature. When a general concept is considered as one of these and as something that can help us reach knowledge, it becomes a subject of logic. Logic then studies the features that necessarily follow from it. Necessity, impossibility, and possibility also serve as conditions under which second- and third-order concepts become subjects of logic. For example, once general philosophy establishes that a universal can be necessary, possible, or impossible—a universal considered under those conditions becomes a subject of logic. The same applies to the subjects of other sciences: a higher science establishes that they exist in the sense needed for them to be studied as subjects, while the science below it explains what they are. This also suggests that a thing exists before its nature is defined, and that what a maker directly brings about is existence, not nature. This is the point we are discussing.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01089

We can describe real things in different ways. Whiteness is a feature present in a white thing. Blindness is different: we recognise it from what the thing lacks. In either case, the description depends on the thing as it really exists. In our view, though, only existence itself is directly present outside the mind. A nature is present there only by being one with some mode of existence.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01090

Other features have no existence outside the mind in either of these ways. Their existence is only as a mental feature of something that exists in the mind, such as treating “human being” as a species or individual people as particulars. When we say that Zayd is particular in reality, we do not mean that there is an external feature called “particularity” attached to him. Nor do we mean that Zayd, as he exists outside the mind, is particular in the mind’s view.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01091

In this broader sense, such concepts are not confined to statements about our thoughts. Sometimes what they describe is a nature simply as it is, not as an idea in the mind or as an object outside it. This is so with features that necessarily follow from a nature, even if the mind is where we consider them. Statements such as “a nature is possible” and “four is even” are true statements about the nature itself. Logical second-order concepts are part of this broader group, but statements made with them are only mental. By contrast, the broader, philosophical sense can be used in statements that are true of things or in statements that exist only in the mind.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01092

Let me add a point. Some thinkers allow a thing to be truly described by a feature that does not exist in itself. One eminent scholar explains that for something to be described “outside” or “in the mind” means that the thing being described exists in that setting in a way that makes the description true of it. This requires the thing itself to exist there; the feature does not need to. It is enough for the thing to exist in a way that lets the mind draw that feature from it. The same applies to being described in the mind. For example, “human being” is universal because its existence in the mind lets the mind draw the feature of universality from it.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01093

On this account, to say that a feature belongs to something means that the thing exists in a way that lets us recognise that feature in it. The feature need not exist separately. That was the scholar’s account. It has several problems. The truth is that being described is a relation between two things that differ in how they exist in that setting. To say that one side exists there but the other does not is arbitrary.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01094

Things do differ in how fully they exist, and each has its own share of existence. Every feature has a level of existence and effects of its own. This includes relations, absences, and powers or capacities. They have a weak share of existence, and a thing can be described by them only when they exist for it.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01095

This applies to every feature. If whiteness is not really present in a body, we cannot truthfully call that body white. The same applies when we say an animal is blind or the sky is above the earth. In books such as The Healing and The Completion, scholars ask: “If a feature does not exist, how can something nonexistent belong to a thing?” They mean that something with no existence in itself cannot exist for something else. But this does not disprove the claim that things can be described by relations, absences, and capacities. As we have seen, these features exist in a limited way, but they still exist. That is enough to make the descriptions true. The corresponding lack of existence prevents a thing from having that feature.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01096

Sometimes a feature’s share in existence is stronger than that of the thing described by it. This is so when prime matter receives bodily and natural forms, and whenever matter receives a form, as we will explain later. So there is no basis for requiring the subject to exist while not requiring the feature to exist, as this scholar does. Someone could just as easily reverse the claim. Since this account does not require either side to exist, another thinker could say that being described in any setting means that the feature has a mode of existence there that lets us judge it of the subject, whether the feature is added to the subject or drawn from it. They could then argue, using the same reasoning, that the feature must exist in that setting but the subject need not.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01097
So the distinction this scholar makes between the subject and its feature—saying that one exists and the other does not—is unsound.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01098

Keep one point in mind. If, by God's grace, you understand that things exist at different levels of fullness and strength, you can answer a serious objection raised against the great philosophers by those whose understanding is limited. They define wisdom as knowledge of real things as they are outside the mind. Yet they also study concepts drawn from other concepts, along with seven kinds of relationships between things.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01099

Remember that every thing has its own level of existence, with its own degree of appearance and actuality. The highest is God: self-sufficient, necessary in Himself, and dependent on nothing. He is pure actuality, free from any trace of possibility, limitation, or lack. Everything else has some degree of essential possibility and limitation. The farther a thing is from the source of existence and necessity, the more limited it is and the more possibility it has.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01100

At the lowest level, a thing’s existence as a substance depends entirely on the form present in it. Its actuality is nothing but potentiality and readiness. Its unity as one thing is also, in one respect, a multiplicity of separate parts, and in another, a unity of connected parts. If substances can have such limited existence, how much weaker must the existence of their features be? These descend through ever weaker degrees of possibility until one feature has no reality beyond its longing and movement toward another feature—of quality, place, or position. It moves toward that other feature in stages and over time. This is the kind of existence motion has in the outside world. If first philosophy accepts motion as real, it must accept this kind of existence, which fits the world outside the mind. To claim that motion has some other, fixed kind of existence is ignorance opposed to wisdom.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01101
III. Existence is pure good
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01102

This question becomes clear once we establish that existence is more than an idea in the mind, however obvious that idea may be. Something real corresponds to it outside the mind: the reality of things actually existing.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01103

Later thinkers treated existence as merely the act of existing, spoken of in the abstract. But here existence means what makes something real, whether we are speaking of existence itself or of a thing’s essence. Anyone who says the concept of existence has no reality outside the mind beyond this abstract idea cannot rightly claim that existence is pure good.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01104

Good is what reasonable people value, what things desire and seek, and what they are drawn to by nature, choice, and instinct. Things do not seek an abstract word or an idea that exists only in the mind. This is so clear that even the simplest mind should see it without having to reason it out.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01105

When we see each thing’s existence as the way it appears—given by God, the One who exists necessarily, who brings natures out of the darkness of nonexistence and into the light of existence—we can see that goodness truly belongs to existence. Existence may be free of evil or mixed with it. Evil is a shortfall in a thing’s existence, or its complete absence. Evil is therefore always a kind of absence: either a thing itself is absent, or it lacks some perfection or good quality. Evil has no reality of its own.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01106

Possible essences and the fixed forms held in the mind are neither good nor evil in themselves; considered on their own, they are neither existent nor nonexistent. As we have explained, the existence attributed to them is their goodness, and their nonexistence is their evil. So existence is pure good, and nonexistence pure evil. The fuller and more complete a thing’s existence, the greater its goodness.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01107

The greatest good in every respect is existence with no absence; full actuality with no unrealized potential; truth without falsehood; necessity rather than mere possibility; perfection without deficiency; and lastingness without change or renewal. The closer another being comes to this highest good, the greater the good it possesses. From there the order descends, step by step, to beings whose existence is weaker and less complete. This continues until we reach the lowest level: prime matter. It has no independent existence of its own; it is real only as the possibility underlying other things. It is “complete” only in its incompleteness, “noble” only in its lowliness. It acts by receiving, takes shape through its indeterminacy, and is distinguished only by its broad kind. We will prove this later. Prime matter is the source of evils and absences, the basis of deficiencies and pains. Yet it is also the net that catches rational souls—the heavenly birds held in cages made from the elements.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01108

Things remain good, both in themselves and in what follows from them, until the order of existence reaches the world of space, time, and conflict. But when this chain reaches the world of bodies and darkness, the crowded confines of material life, some forms of existence—though good in themselves and beneficial to the things they suit—are called evil in relation to what they harm, distress, or destroy. They bring about the loss of a thing itself or of one of its perfections. So evil in itself is one of these two kinds of absence. Existence, simply as existence, is not evil; as you have seen, it is pure good.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01109

True evil is never sought in itself. Relative evil follows by accident from something truly good, which is sought in itself: existence in its own nature. What follows from a thing’s nature is not brought about separately by the one who causes it. As we have said, evils arise from the limits of individual things and from existence falling short of the fullest perfection and greatest beauty.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01110
IV. Existence has no opposite or equal
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01111

Two opposites must belong to the same kind of thing, though not to the broadest class of all. But, as we will explain, existence itself belongs to no such class. So existence, simply as existence, has no opposite. A pair of opposites must also differ as much as possible. But two existences, considered simply as existences, do not differ in that way. Nor does the general nature of existence differ from any idea that can exist. No reality is more general than existence, so that existence could fall under it together with other things and share its features. For this reason, existence itself has no equal or likeness either.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01112

Specific existences, however, can oppose or resemble one another because they are distinguished by meanings and concepts beyond existence itself. So existence, simply as existence, has no opposite and no equal. How could it? Opposites and like things are all existents: they either differ or match. But existence exists through itself, not through something added to it. It therefore stands apart from all the realities whose opposites or likenesses are found among their members. Nothing is like it. Through existence, opposites become real and likenesses are formed. Existence itself appears in the form of opposites and shows itself in things that resemble one another, and in all other things. These differences belong only to the ways existence is limited and appears in different forms. In existence itself, all such differences fade, and all aspects come together. Every pair of opposing or similar features is absorbed into existence itself; the difference lies only in how the mind considers it.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01113

Some raise this objection: if everything shares in existence, then even what we call its opposite or its equal must exist. That would mean opposites or equals exist together, actually or potentially, or that one could apply to the other. This argument fails. We do not accept that existence applies to every idea in every sense. It does not apply to nonexistence as nonexistence, though it may apply to the idea of nonexistence as one of our thoughts. If someone says existence has an opposite or equal, that opposite or equal cannot be found in existence or even imagined as existence itself; it can only be discussed as one idea among others. The rule about sharing a broad kind then does not apply, so the claim has not been proved. It is not obviously absurd, in any case, to say that a feature can be attributed to the thing it opposes.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01114

To continue: the idea of existence differs in meaning from other ideas, but it is not incompatible with them. Every idea has some reality, either outside the mind or in it. Even negative descriptions, though they refer to nonexistence, are in one respect tied to existence. Thus every distinct aspect or conflicting feature traces back in some way to the reality of existence. The fact that incompatible things do not exist together in the outside world—which is only one level of existence—does not prevent them from coming together in existence itself, considered simply as existence.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01115

Existence is opposed to nonexistence, but not to the idea of nonexistence itself. Considered as an idea, nonexistence can be present in the mind, just like any other general idea. What existence cannot cover is not an idea but what the mind supposes the idea refers to: nonexistence, or something nonexistent, as though it were real. There is nothing to say about such a thing; it is neither a thing nor an idea. The mind invents an object for the idea of nonexistence and judges that imagined object to be false and impossible. It does not reject the idea itself, which is present in the mind. This applies to absolute nonexistence and to specific kinds of nonexistence too. There is one further point: a specific absence, like blindness, must belong to some thing, just as the corresponding capacity for sight does.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01116

Absolute existence applies to anything real in any way. Its opposite is absolute nonexistence, which denies every kind of existence. Yet the two can be present together without being opposites, as when we imagine the idea of something absolutely nonexistent. In that thought, we have stripped it of every kind of existence. But the thought itself is still a kind of existence, and stripping it of existence is itself a relation in thought. This idea is therefore not fully stripped of thought: thinking is existence in the mind, so this imagined thing is one instance of existence. See how the light of existence reaches everywhere, even to every idea and meaning, including “nothing,” absolute nonexistence, and the impossible—when we consider them as ideas in the mind, not as actual absences.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01117

We have already distinguished two ways of saying that something belongs to a thing: because it expresses what that thing is, or because it is a description we can truly apply to it. This distinction answers the problem of the absolutely unknown and similar cases. Here we can say that the mind can imagine every idea, even its own nonexistence, the nonexistence of nonexistence, absolute nonexistence, what does not exist in the mind, and all impossible things. It can consider the absolutely unknown, two contradictory ideas, or a word whose meaning depends on its place in a phrase. The mind can then say that the absolutely unknown cannot be described, that contradictions cannot both be true, and that such a word cannot stand alone. But the mind does not imagine the actual reality of the absolutely unknown, the actual joining of contradictions, a real instance of a preposition, a real instance of absolute nonexistence, or a partner to God.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01118

Anything the mind pictures is either a possible thing or an idea that exists in the mind. We apply a label to it only as an idea, not as a real example of what the label names. We do not say, in the ordinary sense, that any of these imagined things is a real contradiction, absolute nonexistence, or a partner to God. These ideas do not name any fixed nature in the mind or outside it. Rather, the mind supposes that some thing is an example of one of these ideas, even though such a thing would be impossible by its very nature. Because the mind pictures the idea as applying to that imagined thing, it judges that the thing cannot be described or spoken of, cannot exist, or cannot have a meaning on its own. These are not firm, direct claims. They work like conditional claims, where neither side is true.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01119

The idea of the absolutely unknown, for example, can be described when we speak of the idea itself, even though the rule that nothing can be said applies to what the mind supposes it refers to. The same applies to absolute nonexistence and to any idea whose own nature does not appear in the mind—whether because it is empty and false, or because it is so complete and real that the mind cannot contain it. For example, when we say that God’s knowledge is identical with His essence, this claim does not apply to the idea of God in our minds, since His essence is not present to us in its full reality. The ideas we have of His true attributes are only ideas. Their unity with His essence applies not to those ideas, but to the reality that reason points to, beyond the limits of mind or imagination.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01120

Consider first what it means to call something completely unknown. We mean that it cannot be known in any way—not even as something we are thinking about. Seen in that way, nothing can be said about it. But since this very act of considering it is a kind of knowing, the idea is mixed with knowledge even as it denies knowledge. This is why it is possible to say that nothing can be said about it, though the impossibility of describing it applies only to what the mind supposes it refers to.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01121

The same is true of absolute nonexistence. The idea means stripping something of every kind of existence, both outside the mind and within it. That is why no claim can be made about it. Yet simply considering or imagining something—even by imagining that it is not considered or imagined—is one way it exists in the mind. In this respect, it has existence; in another, it is treated as having none. These two sides let us make a claim about it and also deny that claim. Tusi makes the same point in Naqd al-Muhassal (Critique of the Summary): “The removal of all existence, both outside the mind and within it, can be imagined as what is not established or imagined at all. We can make a claim about it as the thing we have imagined, but not as something that is not established. This is not a contradiction, because the subject is different in each case. Nor is there any bar to something being the opposite of one thing in one respect and part of it in another. For example, if we say that something is either present in the mind or not present in the mind, what is not present in the mind is the opposite of what is present there, because it is formed by adding ‘not’ to ‘present in the mind.’ Yet as an idea, it is itself part of what is present in the mind.”
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01122
V. Nonexistence is one concept
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01123

Nonexistence, considered in itself, has one simple meaning. We can distinguish one absence from another only by connecting each to something different. In reality or in imagination, there are no separate kinds of nonexistence, each belonging to a different nonexistent thing, nor are there many kinds of negation for the many things that are denied. Whatever lies in the realm of nonexistence and hidden nothingness is alike in being nonexistent. Just as something that does not exist in a given setting is nothing there, so too nonexistence itself is nothing.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01124

Differences among absences come from the things and qualities they are related to. The mind pictures things or states that differ—cause and effect, a condition and what depends on it, or a pair of opposites—and connects the idea of nonexistence to them. Then the absence of a cause differs from the absence of its effect, because the first can bring about the second. The absence of a condition differs from the absence of the thing that depends on it, because without the condition that thing cannot exist. In the same way, the absence of one opposite makes room for the other. Apart from these relationships, one absence does not differ from another. There is no separate nonexistence for each thing, nor one nonexistent thing distinct from another. The imagination sees that a hand differs from a foot and wrongly concludes that the absence of one must differ from the absence of the other. If that were true, every thing would have infinitely many separate absences, piled on top of one another without end.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01125

Some philosophers speak of an endless chain of absences, such as the absences associated with events without end. But they mean that we can always imagine another step backward. They do not mean that an infinite chain of separate absences actually exists. Whatever we actually work through is finite, though there is no one point at which we must stop.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01126

The mind divides nonexistence by relating it to many things: the absence of this thing, then the absence of that thing. This is like dividing one continuous length into one part and another. We can imagine the parts separated and say that one comes before another in position, while the whole comes before its parts by nature. In the same way, we can speak of earlier and later absences when one is the cause of another.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01127

An endless division of a continuous length means there is no final piece so small that we cannot imagine dividing it further. In the same way, an endless sequence of absences means there is no final absence that prevents us from imagining another one before it as its cause. It does not mean there is an actually infinite chain of separate things.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01128

Nonexistence, then, is one and has no distinct parts or form of its own. Nothing in reality is itself nonexistence. If we ask what nonexistence is, there is nothing to name; and if we ask what a thing is, nonexistence cannot be the answer. To call something nonexistent is simply to say that existence does not apply to it. When nonexistence is said of a thing, this means that existence is not said of it. The thing does not acquire a piece of nonexistence.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01129
VI. How the absence of a cause and the absence of its effect relate to each other
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01130

Nonexistence, simply as nonexistence, cannot be understood, any more than it can exist. Yet the human mind can form an idea of anything and use that idea as a label. Just as it forms ideas of the natures of things that exist outside the mind, it also forms ideas for things that have no real nature of their own. These ideas apply to their supposed examples only by assumption, as we explained earlier.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01131

Absences and things that exist only in thought become distinct through what the mind connects them with. To think of the absence of a particular thing, we must first think of that thing. Once held in thought, it can be judged in different ways, including as cause or effect. So we can say that the absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect, but not that the absence of an effect causes the absence of its cause—even though we can infer from the missing effect that its cause is absent.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01132

The key is to distinguish two ways in which the absence of a cause can be called a cause. First, because the idea of the cause’s absence is present in the mind, the mind can judge it to be a cause, even if that is not what the judgment truly refers to. What the judgment truly describes as the cause is the cause’s absence itself—not the mental picture or idea of that absence. We can make this judgment only when the idea is present in the mind.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01133

Second, the idea of the cause’s absence in the mind itself brings about the idea of the effect’s absence there. But the absence of an effect causes the absence of its cause only in this second sense: we infer the cause’s absence from the effect’s absence. So the absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect both in reality and in thought; the absence of an effect leads us to the absence of its cause only in thought, as evidence.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01134

As absences themselves, one is specifically the cause and the other its effect, though we judge them through the mind’s reflection of them. As mental pictures, whichever one appears first can lead to the other, so there is no circular reasoning. Just as the existence of a cause brings about the existence of its effect, while the effect’s existence gives us evidence of its cause, so the absence of a cause brings about the absence of its effect, while the effect’s absence gives us evidence that the cause is absent. If the cause is absent, its effect must be absent too. But the effect’s absence does not prove that the cause is absent. The cause may be absent along with its effect, which would explain why the effect is absent. So the effect is absent with, and because of, the cause’s absence. The cause is absent along with the effect’s absence, but not because of it.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01135
VII. How nonexistence applies to itself
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01136

We can speak of nonexistence just as we speak of anything else. For example, we can say that nonexistence does not exist outside the mind. But this raises a puzzle. When we speak of the absence of something, we name a particular kind of absence. At the same time, that absence is the opposite of the thing whose absence it is. So if we attach it to itself—if we speak of the absence of nonexistence—does it become both a kind and an opposite at once? Those roles seem to conflict: being a kind means the idea applies to its subject, while being an opposite means it excludes what it opposes.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01137

Keep in mind that the relation between nonexistence and the thing it is said to belong to exists only in the mind. Yet the mind’s act of relating nonexistence to something shows that the thing is absent or destroyed. The thing it is said of, as pictured in the mind, gives the idea of nonexistence its limit: it makes the idea definite, and is present in thought along with it. So nonexistence tied to that thing is a particular kind of nonexistence. But when this idea names a thing that has been ruined or destroyed by nonexistence, it stands opposite to that thing.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01138

These two relations apply in different ways. Being a kind is a relation among ideas in the mind, like other logical ideas. Being opposite is a relation among things outside the mind, even though the mind can hold both opposites together as ideas. This explanation untangles the issue better than some later philosophers’ accounts.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01139
VIII. A nonexistent thing cannot be restored
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01140

Nonexistence means only that existence is absent. Since existence is a thing’s very identity, one individual can have only one identity—and therefore one existence and one nonexistence. The same individual cannot exist twice or be absent twice. This is what the mystics mean when they say that God never reveals Himself in the same form twice. It follows that something which has ceased to exist cannot return as exactly the same individual. If its identity really were the same, its existence would have to be the same too. Yet the argument treats that single existence as occurring more than once. It would be both one and many, which is a contradiction. It would also mean that the beginning and the return were the same state, though they are opposites. That is impossible.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01141

If the beginning and return are no different, then the first return cannot be distinguished from a second, or a third from a fourth, and so on. Once one return is allowed, infinitely many returns would be possible, with no reason to stop at one point rather than another. This is plainly false. The same reasoning applies to saying that one and the same thing can be absent more than once.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01142

You might object: many events that happen in time do not exist, then exist, then cease to exist. So the same thing has two absences. If this is allowed for absence, why not allow more than one existence too? The answer is that we have already explained what it means for nonexistence to be attributed to something: the thing is wholly absent. There is no real subject that exists while nonexistence is added to it or drawn from it. The mind pictures a thing and applies the idea of nonexistence to it. So absences multiply in thought only when the things they are related to differ. There is no individual thing before its existence or after it that we can call one, many, or identical. The mind simply relates absence to a nature whose existence is limited to a certain time, before or after that time.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01143

To say that a thing did not exist before it came to be, or will not exist after it ceases, means that its existence has a limited span. Its capacity to exist does not extend into earlier or later times. Nonexistence itself is one; it is not, in itself, earlier or later. The mind’s imagination pictures a temporal event as having an endless absence before it, then existence, then a later absence—as if these were two ends with the event between them.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01144

Ordinary imagination goes further. It pictures nonexistence as something that arrives, removes a thing’s existence from reality, and wipes its identity away. They overlook that the existence of things consists in ways the True Source reveals Himself, like rays from the First Source’s light. Each of these appearances remains what it is; it does not turn into another. Someone whose view is too limited to take in the whole thinks that each one disappears from existence and is replaced by another. But consider what it would mean for nonexistence to overtake something that is real. It would have to happen either at the very level and time where that thing exists, which would bring opposites together at once, or outside that level and time. Yet a thing can exist only at its own level, where it becomes real and appears. Each thing has its own mode and place in existence, with the qualities, times, and places that belong to it. These do not move from it to something else. Since each thing has only the one mode of existence its prior causes and conditions give it, there is no other state of being for nonexistence to enter and erase, or to take over in its place.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01145

When people say that possible things do not resist nonexistence, even while they exist, they mean this: if we set aside external causes and the ways the First Real appears, and consider each possible nature or idea by itself, its meaning does not prevent things beyond its own nature from being added or removed—including existence and nonexistence. This is because existence does not rest on these limited natures themselves. But consider how God gives existence, reveals Himself through His names and attributes, and preserves each thing for the span known to His knowledge, which encompasses everything. Seen in that light, the thing cannot cease or be destroyed. To allow that something can cease at one level of reality is a mistake of the imagination.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01146

This is the full account from the viewpoint of the mystics. Here are some arguments from the more familiar philosophical tradition. They should be enough for a reader with a sound mind, unless bias or stubbornness gets in the way. Some regard it as self-evident that a nonexistent thing cannot be restored. Avicenna said so, and al-Razi approved his view: “Anyone who returns to a sound nature and frees himself from bias will see clearly that restoring a nonexistent thing is impossible.”
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01147

The first argument is this: if the very same nonexistent thing were restored, nonexistence would have to come between the thing and itself. It would then exist before itself in time. That would be like a thing being prior to itself by nature, which would mean circular causation. Since this result is clearly false, the claim that led to it must also be false.
Stage Two: Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01148

The reply is that the argument wrongly treats two different times as one. It means only that nonexistence comes between the two times when the thing exists, and that the thing’s earlier and later existence are viewed from two different times. This does not mean there are two individuals.
